title: Merge related tables
goal: Connect tables by a key and audit which records matched.
prerequisites: Use column selection and understand unique Student_ID values.

cells.title: Attach the department
cells.explanation: The Program column is a key shared by two tables. A many-to-one merge lets several students match one department row. The validation checks that the lookup table has only one row per program.
cells.code:
df = students()
result = df.merge(departments(), on="Program", how="left", validate="many_to_one")
print(result[["Student_ID", "Program", "Department"]])

questions.answer: Match the two tables using Program values.

questions.prompt: Will the result contain 2 rows or 12 rows?
questions.answer: 12 rows, one for each student, because each Program matches exactly one lookup row.
Students may repeat a Program, but each Program must appear at most once in the lookup table.

cells.task: Use DataFrame.join to attach the same lookup fields. Set Program as the lookup index and keep the student index.
cells.solution:
df = students()
lookup = departments().set_index("Program")
result = df.join(lookup, on="Program", how="left", validate="many_to_one")
print(result[["Student_ID", "Program", "Department"]])
cells.solution_note: join can use the right table index as the key. Both forms preserve all 12 students here.

check.prompt: Which side must have unique Program values?
check.feedback: The lookup side must be unique for many-to-one matching.

cells.watch: Do not join tables by row position when they describe entities identified by keys.
cells.takeaway: Choose and validate the matching key.

cells.title: Keep matches or keep every student
cells.explanation: An inner merge keeps only keys found in both tables. A left merge keeps every key from the left table. In this complete assessment lookup, a missing Quiz comes from an unmatched student. With other data, a matched assessment could itself have a missing Quiz; use the merge indicator to test for unmatched records.
cells.code:
result = students().merge(assessment(), on="Student_ID", how="inner", validate="one_to_one")
print(result[["Student_ID", "Name", "Quiz"]])
print("Rows:", len(result))

questions.prompt: Which registered student disappears from the inner merge?
questions.answer: S012, Lina, because the assessment table has no S012 row.

questions.prompt: Does an unmatched quiz mean the student earned zero?
questions.answer: No. A missing match is unknown and needs investigation.

cells.task: Change the merge to left and store the full merged table in merged. Select only students whose Quiz is missing into result, keeping Student_ID, Name, and Quiz, then print result.
cells.solution:
merged = students().merge(assessment(), on="Student_ID", how="left", validate="one_to_one")
result = merged.loc[merged["Quiz"].isna(), ["Student_ID", "Name", "Quiz"]]
print(result)
cells.solution_note: The left merge retains 12 students; the missing-match report contains only S012.

check.prompt: Which merge preserves every registered student?
options: left, with students on the left
right, with assessments on the right
check.feedback: A left merge preserves the left table keys even when there is no right-side match.

cells.verify:
assert len(result) == 11
assert "S012" not in result["Student_ID"].tolist()
cells.watch: Filling an unmatched assessment with zero changes its meaning; agree on a policy first.
cells.takeaway: Merge type determines which records remain.

cells.title: Audit both unmatched sides
cells.explanation: An outer merge keeps keys from either table. indicator=True adds a _merge column showing left_only, right_only, or both. This is a simple way to find records that need review.
cells.code:
audit = students().merge(assessment(), on="Student_ID", how="outer", indicator=True, validate="one_to_one")
result = audit.loc[audit["_merge"].ne("both"), ["Student_ID", "_merge"]]
print(result)
print("All merged rows:", len(audit))

questions.answer: The key exists in assessments but not in the student table.

questions.prompt: Which IDs will the audit show?
questions.answer: S012 is left_only; S013 is right_only.
One side can reveal missing assessments; the other can reveal assessments for an unregistered or mistyped ID.

cells.task: Use a right merge instead. Keep indicator=True and report the row that has no registered student name.
cells.hint: A right merge preserves the assessment keys; inspect Name.isna().
cells.solution:
audit = students().merge(assessment(), on="Student_ID", how="right", indicator=True, validate="one_to_one")
result = audit.loc[audit["Name"].isna(), ["Student_ID", "_merge"]]
print(result)
print("All merged rows:", len(audit))
cells.solution_note: The right merge keeps 12 assessment records. S013 remains even though no student profile matches.

check.prompt: How many distinct keys does the outer merge contain?
check.feedback: The union contains S001 through S013: 11 shared keys plus 2 unmatched keys.

cells.watch: Pandas may match missing keys to other missing keys; audit or reject null keys before important merges.
cells.takeaway: Use indicator to make unmatched records visible.

cells.title: Stop duplicate-key expansion
cells.explanation: If a lookup repeats a key, one input row can produce several output rows. The code deliberately adds a duplicate AI lookup. Catching MergeError lets us demonstrate the problem without stopping the lesson.
cells.code:
bad_lookup = pd.concat([departments(), departments().iloc[[0]]], ignore_index=True)
blocked = False
try:
    students().merge(bad_lookup, on="Program", validate="many_to_one")
except pd.errors.MergeError:
    blocked = True
    print("Blocked: Program is not unique in the lookup.")
result = students().merge(bad_lookup, on="Program")
print("Rows without validation:", len(result))

questions.answer: To catch the expected validation error and continue the lesson.

questions.prompt: How many rows appear without validation?
questions.answer: 18: each of the 6 AI students matches twice, and the 6 IT students match once.

questions.prompt: Should every duplicate key be dropped automatically?
questions.answer: No. Repeated keys may describe different facts. This example repeats an identical lookup row, so removing that exact duplicate is justified.

cells.task: Remove only exact duplicate lookup rows, confirm Program is unique, and perform the validated merge.
cells.hint: drop_duplicates() removes exact repeats; is_unique checks the key.
cells.solution:
bad_lookup = pd.concat([departments(), departments().iloc[[0]]], ignore_index=True)
lookup = bad_lookup.drop_duplicates()
assert lookup["Program"].is_unique
result = students().merge(lookup, on="Program", validate="many_to_one")
print("Validated rows:", len(result))
cells.solution_note: The duplicated lookup was identical, so removing the exact repeat restores 12 rows.

check.prompt: What can repeated keys on both sides cause?
check.feedback: Each matching pair produces a row, so duplicate keys can expand the result.

cells.watch: validate checks the relationship; it does not decide how to repair conflicting records.
cells.takeaway: Check key uniqueness before trusting merged row counts.
